name: Iran
card_headline: Eight months into war with the US and Israel, Iran has no ceasefire, has loaded no crude since August and negotiates through Qatar with no deal
card_summary: The US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February and killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. A June memorandum broke down by August and the US blockade of Iranian ports is back. Strikes still pass between US and Iranian forces around Qeshm Island and the Gulf, while Qatar and Pakistan mediate. The rial passed 2 million to the dollar in August, official inflation ran above 80 percent over the summer, and the IAEA cannot locate Iran's highly enriched uranium. Rights groups count at least 532 executions this year.
card_local: Local sourcing is thin: no free domestic press was read, so this draft uses the state-aligned Tasnim agency and the diaspora outlets Iran International and IranWire. Tasnim carries Iran's UN mission in Vienna saying inspections cannot return to normal under attack, and Iran International reports Qatar saying mediation has gained momentum. [1][2]
card_international: Reuters reported on 2 November that Qatari-mediated talks ended with altered proposals and no breakthrough, and Al Jazeera reported US and Iranian strikes around Qeshm Island on 17 and 18 November. [3][4]
card_scholar: Critical Threats (AEI and ISW) assesses that international recognition of Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz is one Iranian war aim, and the Arms Control Association finds no sign that Iran is weaponizing. [5][6]
context_md: Iran stopped letting IAEA monitors review its nuclear sites after US and Israeli strikes in June 2025. [7] Protests that began in late December 2025 over the falling currency spread nationwide, and Reuters says they were crushed last winter. [8][9] The US and Israel launched the present war on 28 February 2026, and the first strikes killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. [3][9] His son Mojtaba Khamenei is now supreme leader but has not appeared in public since the strike, according to Al Jazeera. [10] A two-week ceasefire took effect on 8 April, and the US naval blockade of Iranian ports was in place by 22 April. [11] Trump and President Masoud Pezeshkian signed a memorandum in June that extended the ceasefire and lifted the blockade, [12] but US strikes resumed on 7 and 8 July and Trump reinstated the blockade on 13 July. [13][14]

sections.title: No ceasefire: US and Iranian forces still trade strikes while Qatar and Pakistan mediate
sections.body_md:
The war began on 28 February, when US and Israeli strikes killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. [9] A two-week ceasefire took effect on 8 April, and President Trump later extended it with no end date while the US naval blockade of Iranian ports stayed in place. [11] On 17 and 18 June Trump and President Masoud Pezeshkian signed a memorandum that extended the ceasefire by 60 days and lifted the blockade. [12] It did not last. The US struck dozens of Iranian targets on 7 and 8 July after attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, [13] and on 13 July Trump reinstated the blockade. [14] Sources date the end of the memorandum differently: AP's account says Trump called the interim deal over in early July, while Al Jazeera later wrote that it collapsed in August. [14][15]

Fighting has continued at lower intensity. On 2 November US forces struck Qeshm Island, a main base for Iranian naval forces, which US officials called a defensive action. [16] The IRGC claimed radar strikes on a US base in Bahrain on 13, 15 and 17 November, and US Central Command denied that the 17 November strike hit US equipment. [5] On 18 November Iran's Foreign Ministry said it hit US assets at two Gulf bases after another US strike on Qeshm, and the page's headline reported Kuwait and Bahrain intercepting attacks. [4]

Qatar is the main mediator, and Pakistan's army chief, Asim Munir, has visited Tehran several times. [15] Reuters reported on 2 November that several days of indirect talks with Qatari mediators ended with altered proposals and no breakthrough. It described a condensed version of Iran's September seven-step plan, which Trump had rejected: the US ends its blockade, Iran reopens Hormuz, Washington waives oil sanctions and cancels new ones, and nuclear talks follow. [3] Qatar's foreign ministry said on 10 November that mediation had gained momentum, [2] while Iran's security chief said no talks with the US were under way. [17] Iran International's headline list says Trump said on 22 November he was inclined to resume strikes after the new year if there is no deal. This draft could not corroborate that item. [18]

lenses.local: Iran International reported on 10 November that Qatar saw mediation gaining momentum, and relayed a state TV commentator saying Tehran would discuss the nuclear file only after Washington accepts Iran's seven conditions and the war ends. [2][19]
lenses.international: Reuters reports talks that ended without a breakthrough, and Al Jazeera reports continued US and Iranian strikes around Qeshm Island and the Gulf. [3][16][4]
lenses.scholar: Critical Threats (AEI and ISW) assesses that securing recognition of Iranian control over Hormuz is an Iranian war aim and found nothing significant to report on US and Iran talks on 17 November. [5]

sections.title: The nuclear file: no inspections of bombed sites, a stockpile the IAEA cannot locate and a referral to the Security Council
sections.body_md:
Iran stopped letting IAEA monitors review its nuclear sites after the US and Israeli strikes of June 2025. A restricted IAEA report circulated on 13 November says the agency cannot verify the location or status of about 972 pounds (roughly 440 kg) of highly enriched uranium, or of about 18,958 pounds of lower-enriched material, and cannot rule out diversion of declared material. Inspectors visited the Bushehr plant twice in the past three months but have gathered no information on Iran's other declared facilities. [7] Iran International, citing a report Reuters saw, says the agency does not know where Iran's newest enrichment plant is or whether it holds nuclear material. [20]

On 9 September the IAEA Board of Governors voted 23 to 3, with eight abstentions, to report Iran to the UN Security Council, the first such referral in 20 years. Russia, China and Niger opposed it. [6][21] Al Jazeera notes that Council action is unlikely because Russia and China hold vetoes. [21] The Arms Control Association adds that Iranian lawmakers have submitted a bill to withdraw from the NPT, that Pezeshkian has said Iran does not want nuclear weapons, and that Iran shows no sign of weaponization or of digging out bombed material. [6] Iran's UN mission in Vienna said on 14 November that normal safeguards cannot resume under abnormal circumstances. [1]

Two single-outlet reports bear on what comes next. Iran International says the Assembly of Experts, which selects the supreme leader, has called for a review of Iran's defence doctrine that could open the way to reversing the religious ban on nuclear weapons. It also reports that Pakistan's army chief floated letting Iran enrich to 3.67 percent while diluting or converting about 400 kg of its 60 percent uranium, in return for partial release of frozen assets and the return of inspectors. US acceptance is unconfirmed. [19] Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, has said Iran is weighing a change to its nuclear doctrine, and Trump has named the suspected underground site Pickaxe Mountain as a target still to be dealt with. [15]

lenses.local: Tasnim, a state-aligned agency, carries Iran's position that inspections cannot normalise under attack, and Iran International reports the doctrine review. [1][19]
lenses.international: Bloomberg reports the IAEA's inability to account for the stockpile, and Al Jazeera reports the referral vote. [7][21]
lenses.scholar: The Arms Control Association records the NPT withdrawal bill, the lack of excavation at bombed sites and no sign of weaponization. [6]

sections.title: Oil and the blockade: Iran has loaded no crude since 25 August and Hormuz traffic is a fraction of normal
sections.body_md:
Kpler analyst Homayoun Falakshahi reports that Iran has not loaded a crude or condensate cargo since 25 August. Oil on water outside the blockade zone fell to zero in mid-October from a peak of 88.8 million barrels on 14 July, and about 43 million barrels remain stranded inside the blockade area. Oil sales are about 30 to 40 percent of government revenue, and Kpler expects that revenue to reach zero by mid-December because Chinese buyers usually pay one to two months after discharge. [22]

Before the war about 130 vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz each day, according to Windward data cited by Al Jazeera. [13] Lloyd's List Intelligence counted 550 transits by vessels not linked to Iran in October, up from 504 in September. The two counts use different methods. Lloyd's also reports that US Central Command says 147 commercial vessels have been redirected and five ships disabled, and that the UK maritime security agency UKMTO logged 163 incidents from the start of the conflict to 11 November. [23] On 18 November Iran's army said three oil tankers hit naval mines east of the strait, and the IRGC said the ships ignored its warnings and must coordinate passage with Iranian authorities. [4]

The US is extending the blockade overland. On 8 November US Central Command announced Task Force Iron Gate to target land routes and the Caspian Sea, and Trump wrote that very little gets into or out of Iran. [24] On 15 October the Treasury designated 26 targets in what it called Operation Economic Outcast, including exchange houses and banks in Iran's shadow banking network. [25] Iran International lists a further round of sanctions on 22 entities and eight people on 23 November, which this draft did not corroborate. [18]

lenses.local: Iran International's headline list says Iran called a US land blockade nearly impossible to enforce and denied supply shortages. [18]
lenses.international: Lloyd's List Intelligence and Al Jazeera report the redirected ships, mine strikes and reduced transits. [23][4]
lenses.scholar: Andreas Krieg of King's College London called the task force a desperate attempt to extend the naval blockade by land, and Matthew Savill of RUSI expects reliance on satellite imagery, drones and financial intelligence. [24]

sections.title: Prices: the rial passed 2 million to the dollar, official inflation ran above 80 percent and a gas shortage is coming this winter
sections.body_md:
The rial fell past 2 million to the US dollar on the open market in August, a record low, after Washington announced its toughest sanctions yet. [26] Kpler put the dollar at about 272,000 tomans (2.72 million rials) on 22 October, against 157,000 tomans in mid-June. [22] Al Jazeera compared prices with the pre-war period: cooking oil up 177 percent, baby formula up 95 percent and insulin up 642 percent. It gives the minimum wage for the year ending March 2027 as 166 million rials, about $82 at the time. [26]

Inflation figures differ by agency and month. The Statistical Centre of Iran reported year-on-year inflation of 88.6 percent for 22 May to 21 June, with bread and grain up 138.8 percent, according to AFP. [27] The Central Bank said annual inflation was 83.9 percent in the month to 22 July. [28] Al Jazeera cited the Statistical Center at 89 percent for the month ending 22 August, with food above 127 percent. [29] Patrika, citing unnamed Iranian media, reports 73.6 percent annual inflation on 29 October and an apology from the economy minister; that report names no statistics agency. [30] The IMF projected in April that Iran's economy would shrink 6.1 percent in 2026 with consumer prices up 68.9 percent. [31]

Energy is the next strain. Reuters reports that officials expect this winter's gas shortfall at 430 million cubic metres, against 300 million last year, after early war damage to four processing plants, and that the war has destroyed millions of jobs. [9] On 18 November Pezeshkian called for energy subsidy reform and a crackdown on profiteering, citing the war and the blockade. [4] Iran International's headline list reports that scheduled power cuts resumed on 22 November, that a lawmaker warned they could cost over a million jobs, and that truck drivers struck across the country. Those items were not corroborated here. [18]

lenses.local: IranWire reported in April that people paid about 600,000 tomans per gigabyte of internet and that one source claimed at least 100,000 industrial workers had lost jobs, a figure the article does not verify. [32]
lenses.international: AFP, Reuters and Al Jazeera report inflation above 80 percent, record currency lows and winter gas shortages. [27][29][9]
lenses.scholar: The IMF's April forecast, as reported by Amwal Al Ghad, sees a 6.1 percent contraction in 2026. [31]

sections.title: Repression: a contested protest death toll, record hangings and an 83-day internet blackout
sections.body_md:
Protests that began in late December 2025 with shopkeepers angry over the falling currency spread into a nationwide movement. [8] Counts of the dead differ widely. Iran's Martyrs Foundation, via Press TV, gave 3,117 on 21 January, the first official figure. [8] The US-based group HRANA had verified 6,872 deaths by 4 February, with 11,280 more cases under investigation and more than 50,000 arrests, according to AFP. [33] A UN Human Rights Council fact-finding mission concluded that Iran committed crimes against humanity, said the true toll was significantly higher than Iran's figure of 3,038, and found that at least 58 people had been executed on security charges in 2026. [34] This draft found no Iranian response to that report.

Execution counts also diverge. Iran Human Rights counted at least 532 executions from 1 January to 31 August, including 71 on national security charges, 31 protesters and 14 espionage defendants, and said only 77 were officially announced. It excluded more than 500 further reports it could not verify. [35] The Abdorrahman Boroumand Center counted 901 for January to July plus 28 in August. [36] Human Rights Watch and the Boroumand Center said on 10 September that at least 59 men had been executed in five months, at least 32 of them linked to protests, and that five were hanged in public squares. [37] Amnesty said in April that four men were reportedly executed in secret within 24 hours and that seven protesters faced imminent execution. [38]

On 21 May CPJ and RSF said a nationwide internet blackout had reached 83 days, which NetBlocks called the longest and most severe in Iran, and that it was hiding a crackdown on independent media. The Iranian-American journalist Reza Valizadeh remained in Evin Prison. [39]

lenses.local: Iran International's headline list says two political prisoners whose murder death sentences were overturned were moved to solitary confinement on 22 November, raising fears of execution on another charge. [18]
lenses.international: AFP and Al Jazeera carry the competing protest death counts, and Euronews carries the Boroumand Center's execution count. [33][8][36]
lenses.scholar: The UN fact-finding mission, as reported by the International Business Times, found crimes against humanity against protesters and perceived dissenters. [34]

sections.title: Who rules: an unseen supreme leader, a president who negotiates and a quiet street under heavy deployment
sections.body_md:
Mojtaba Khamenei has not appeared in public since the 28 February strike that wounded him and killed his father and his wife, according to Al Jazeera. Officials attribute his absence to the threat of assassination, and people close to his circle told Reuters he suffered serious injuries including facial damage and harm to one or both legs. Those injury reports are not confirmed. [10] On 3 November Pezeshkian said the supreme leader had given the government "certain authorities" over talks with the US, a shift from June, when the leader said the US could not be trusted. [16]

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi leads the diplomacy, and parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf is described by Al Jazeera as Iran's chief negotiator. [40] Iran International reports that the term of the state broadcaster's chief, Peyman Jebelli, expired nearly two months ago and that who controls state TV is unresolved. [41]

Reuters reported on 16 November that there have been no notable protests against the ruling system since the war began, that security agencies are on alert, and that a senior official called economic hardship "a fire smouldering beneath ashes". [9] Critical Threats reports that security forces were deployed in Tehran on 14 November and Esfahan on 16 November before any protests, that Iran launched a mass mobilisation and training effort called the Janfada Campaign to expand security manpower, and that at least 1,000 people rallied in Abdanan, Ilam Province, on 17 November after a bus crash killed at least 12, with some chants turning to calls for the regime's overthrow. [5]

lenses.local: Iran International reports a dispute over who will lead state TV, one sign of unresolved institutional control. [41]
lenses.international: Reuters reports a quiet street and officials who fear unrest driven by gas shortages and prices. [9]
lenses.scholar: Critical Threats documents preemptive deployments and the Abdanan rally, and Al Jazeera quotes analyst Negar Mortazavi saying the leader's absence is unusual but imposed by circumstance. [5][10]

sections.title: The human cost: casualty figures rest on Iranian authorities, medicines are short and minorities and Afghans carry extra weight
sections.body_md:
The WHO's 15 September situation report cites Iranian national authorities for 3,375 deaths and 33,806 injuries since 28 February, and counts 27 WHO-verified attacks on health care that killed 11 people. It adds that damage to the power grid disrupted hospitals and vaccine cold chains and that shortages of imported medicines hit cancer and chronic-disease patients. WHO does not verify the casualty figures, and this draft found no independent total. [42]

Minorities face a heavier crackdown. Independent UN experts said on 6 August that at least 24 Baluch and 22 Kurds had been executed in 2026, that thousands had been detained since protests began, and that the crackdown intensified after the US and Israeli strikes. They made an urgent appeal for four Kurdish men and one Baluch man facing imminent execution after proceedings that allegedly involved torture. [43] Iran blames the protests on US and Israeli influence and defends the death penalty as lawful, according to the same report. [43]

Afghans are being pushed out. UNHCR says about 492,300 Afghans have been deported from Iran in 2026, about 85 percent of all returns to Afghanistan this year, although the article's other figures for returns from Iran are inconsistent. [44]

lenses.local: IranWire's April account describes residents paying heavily for internet, rising prices and anxiety about income. [32]
lenses.international: VOA and The National report the Afghan deportations and the minority crackdown using UN figures. [44][43]
lenses.scholar: The WHO situation report is the main technical source on attacks on health care and medicine shortages. [42]

sections.title: The region and the great powers: Gulf states under fire, China and Russia against new strikes
sections.body_md:
Reuters reported on 2 November that Iran has repeatedly fired drones and missiles at Gulf states and that fighting has renewed in Yemen. [3] On 18 November Bahrain and Kuwait reported intercepting attacks and Manama blamed Iran. A Houthi spokesman claimed attacks on Riyadh and Saudi airbases, which Saudi Arabia did not confirm. [4]

China and Russia have called against renewed military action, and China's Wang Yi met the Iranian security official Ali Bagheri Kani in Beijing, according to Reuters. [3] Al Jazeera's analysis says US media reported Russia sending drone components and explosives to Iran by way of the Caspian Sea. [24] Al Jazeera's White House correspondent said Iran is expected to feature at a Trump, Xi and Putin meeting on the sidelines of APEC in Shenzhen, with no breakthrough expected. [4]

Mediation runs through Doha, Islamabad and Muscat. The Economic Cooperation Organization welcomed Tehran's proposed two-day ceasefire at a meeting in Islamabad, and Araghchi went on to Oman for talks Al Jazeera cites as constructive and focused on a regional security framework. [40][4] Iran International's headline list says Tehran warned against use of a US-backed transit corridor in Armenia, citing Hormuz. [18]

lenses.local: Iran International's headline list reports Tehran's warning over the Armenian corridor and renewed threats against European bases, with a claimed missile range of 4,500 km that the outlet questions. [18]
lenses.international: Reuters and Al Jazeera report Gulf attacks, Chinese and Russian opposition to new strikes and the mediation channels. [3][4]
lenses.scholar: Al Jazeera's analysts say the task force cannot seal Iran's land borders without Caspian access or troops on the ground. [24]

scores.coverage_basis: Wires, Al Jazeera and think tanks cover the war daily, with live blogs, Reuters and AP copy and a daily Critical Threats update. [4][3][5] Coverage of life inside Iran is thinner because of the internet blackout and press controls, and local sourcing relies on state-aligned and diaspora outlets. [39][1]

severity.basis: An interstate war with no ceasefire continues, with US and Iranian strikes in November and 3,375 deaths reported by Iranian authorities since 28 February. [5][42]
WHO verified 27 attacks on health care and reports medicine shortages and damage to hospital power, though no famine or mass displacement count was found. [42]
A UN fact-finding mission found crimes against humanity in the January crackdown, executions run at 532 to over 900 this year, and the internet was shut for 83 days. [34][35][36][39]

Official inflation ran 84 to 89 percent in mid-year readings, the rial passed 2 million to the dollar, no crude has been loaded since 25 August and the IMF sees a 6.1 percent contraction. [29][26][22][31]
Conditions are worse than a year ago: the war began in February, the June memorandum collapsed, the blockade returned and a winter gas shortage looms. [14][9]

parts.basis: The US is fighting and blockading Iran, China and Russia oppose new strikes, and Gulf states and Pakistan are under fire or mediating. [14][3][4]
Hormuz transits are a fraction of pre-war levels and Qatar says the closure worsens the global energy crisis as winter nears. [23][13][2]
Iran has fired at Gulf states, fighting has renewed in Yemen, and Houthi and Iraqi fronts are active. [3][4][40]
Iran deported about 492,300 Afghans this year, and energy prices reach consumers worldwide, but this draft found no large refugee outflow from Iran. [44][2]
A sitting head of state's killing in a strike, the first IAEA referral to the Security Council in 20 years and an NPT withdrawal bill all test the nonproliferation order. [9][21][6]

summary: Iran matters beyond its borders through the energy chokepoint at Hormuz, a nuclear program that inspectors cannot verify and a war that already reaches Gulf states and Yemen. [23][7][4]
gi.up: A resumed US bombing campaign after the new year, an Iranian move to leave the NPT, or sustained closure of Hormuz through winter.
gi.down: A verified deal that reopens Hormuz, lifts the blockade and returns IAEA inspectors.

gaps: Local sourcing is the weakest part of this draft: Iran has no free domestic press, and the local lens rests on Tasnim (state-aligned) and the diaspora outlets Iran International and IranWire. No Persian-language domestic outlet was read; the one attempted page was blocked.

Everything dated 22 to 24 November comes from Iran International's rolling headline list, read as headlines only, so the Trump statement on resuming strikes, the 23 November sanctions round, the truck drivers' strike and the power cuts are single-sourced and uncorroborated.
The end of the June memorandum is dated differently by AP (early July) and Al Jazeera (August); this draft reports both.
No independent casualty total was found; the 3,375 deaths are Iranian authorities' figures relayed by WHO, and Iranian state, HRANA and OCHA totals for the war were not opened.
Inflation figures come from different agencies, months and measures (88.6, 83.9, 89 and 73.6 percent) and were not reconciled; the 73.6 percent figure is from a secondary outlet.

The IAEA report of 13 November is restricted and was read only through Bloomberg and Iran International; the UN fact-finding report on the January protests was read through a trade-press summary; the IMF forecast through a secondary report.
Execution counts differ by hundreds between Iran Human Rights and the Boroumand Center, and the IHRNGO page contains internal numeric inconsistencies.
Mojtaba Khamenei's injuries and condition are reported by unnamed sources and are unconfirmed.
No Israeli, Gulf-state or Russian official source was read directly, and the Lebanon front, Iraqi militias and the Houthi front are covered only in passing.
Not covered: water scarcity and land subsidence, women's rights and the hijab, the Baha'i community and the details of the Armenia corridor dispute.

Reporter entries are limited to what each byline or profile page shows; documentary availability varies by country; the Hold Your Fire episode page omits the year, which is inferred as 2026 from its subject.

reporters.name: Parisa Hafezi
reporters.bio: Co-bylined the 16 November 2026 Reuters report on Iranian leaders' worry over gas shortages and public mood, and the 2 November report on the stalled Qatar talks.
reporters.why: Her reporting draws on named and unnamed Iranian officials, which makes it one of the few windows into how the leadership sees the economy and unrest.
reporters.label: Reuters via TimesLIVE

reporters.name: Maziar Motamedi
reporters.bio: Co-bylined, with Alia Chughtai and Fatemah Karimkhan, the 26 August 2026 Al Jazeera report on the rial passing 2 million to the dollar.
reporters.why: The report prices everyday goods before and after the war and records wages in dollars.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

reporters.name: Behrouz Turani
reporters.bio: Bylined the 19 November 2026 Iran International report on the contest over who will control Iran's state broadcaster.
reporters.why: Covers institutional infighting in Tehran from outside the country's press controls.
reporters.label: Iran International

reporters.name: Jonathan Tirone
reporters.bio: Bylined the 15 November 2026 Bloomberg report on Iran extending its shutout of IAEA inspectors and the agency's unverified stockpile.
reporters.why: Sets out the IAEA's latest numbers on enriched uranium in one place.
reporters.label: Bloomberg via News Tribune

reporters.name: Kelsey Davenport
reporters.bio: Co-wrote, with Shaghayegh Chris Rostampour, the October 2026 Arms Control Today article on the IAEA board's referral of Iran to the Security Council.
reporters.why: Explains the vote count, the NPT withdrawal bill and what the referral can and cannot do.
reporters.label: Arms Control Association

reporters.name: Homayoun Falakshahi
reporters.bio: Wrote the 22 October 2026 Kpler analysis of Iran's oil on water and the effect of the US blockade.
reporters.why: Gives barrel counts and a revenue timeline for Iran's oil exports.
reporters.label: Kpler

reporters.name: Andreas Krieg
reporters.bio: Quoted by Al Jazeera on 9 November 2026 calling the new US task force an intelligence fusion cell that cannot police Iran's borders.
reporters.why: Gives a security-studies view of whether the blockade can be extended by land.
reporters.label: Al Jazeera

reporters.name: Vali Nasr
reporters.role: Majid Khadduri Professor of International Affairs and Middle East Studies, Johns Hopkins SAIS
reporters.bio: Author of Iran's Grand Strategy: A Political History (Princeton University Press, 2025), per the publisher's page.
reporters.why: Argues that Iran's foreign policy follows a regime-security grand strategy shaped by the Iran-Iraq War and fear of US intentions.
reporters.label: Princeton University Press

reporters.name: Ali Vaez
reporters.bio: Guest on the Hold Your Fire! episode on the US-Israeli war on Iran, where he discusses internet blackouts, succession and the risk of state collapse.
reporters.why: Crisis Group's account of conditions inside Iran early in the war.
reporters.label: Hold Your Fire! podcast

books.title: Iran's Grand Strategy: A Political History
books.author: Vali Nasr
books.why: Draws on memoirs, oral histories and interviews with Iranian decision makers to explain Iran's resistance to the US and its nuclear and regional policy.
books.label: Princeton University Press

books.title: Iran: A Modern History
books.author: Abbas Amanat
books.why: Traces Iran's societies and economies from dynastic change through revolution to the Islamic Republic. The year comes from a Yale News feature dated 25 October 2017.
books.label: Yale News

books.title: A History of Modern Iran
books.author: Ervand Abrahamian
books.why: Covers oil and foreign intervention, the Pahlavi dynasty, the 1979 revolution and the Iran-Iraq war, and won a Choice Outstanding Academic Title award in 2009.
books.label: Cambridge University Press

factchecks.claim: About 3,000 people were killed in Iran's January 2026 protests.
factchecks.by: Iranian authorities (Martyrs Foundation figure of 3,117, carried by Press TV on 21 January)
factchecks.evidence: HRANA had verified 6,872 deaths by 4 February with 11,280 more cases under investigation, and Iran Human Rights confirmed 3,428 before pausing updates; both call their counts minimums. A UN fact-finding mission said the true toll was significantly higher than Iran's own figure of 3,038, so the official numbers also differ from each other.

factchecks.claim: Iran is holding no talks with the United States.
factchecks.by: Iran's security chief, as relayed by Al Jazeera on 9 November
factchecks.evidence: Reuters reported on 2 November that several days of indirect talks with Qatari mediators had ended without a breakthrough while a draft circulated. Qatar's foreign ministry said on 10 November that mediation had gained momentum, and Secretary of State Rubio said talks had never stopped, according to Al Jazeera. The contacts are indirect and mediated, which may explain the denial.

factchecks.claim: Iran carried out about 900 executions in the first seven months of 2026.
factchecks.by: Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights in Iran, as reported by Euronews on 19 August
factchecks.evidence: Iran Human Rights, which verifies each case through two independent sources, counted at least 532 through 31 August and left out more than 500 further reports it could not verify. The gap reflects different verification standards, and only 77 of the 532 were officially announced.

local_md:
Iran International reported on 10 November that Qatar saw mediation gaining momentum, and relayed a state TV commentator saying Tehran would discuss the nuclear file only after Washington accepts Iran's seven conditions and the war ends. [2][19]

Tasnim, a state-aligned agency, carries Iran's position that inspections cannot normalise under attack, and Iran International reports the doctrine review. [1][19]

Iran International's headline list says Iran called a US land blockade nearly impossible to enforce and denied supply shortages. [18]

IranWire reported in April that people paid about 600,000 tomans per gigabyte of internet and that one source claimed at least 100,000 industrial workers had lost jobs, a figure the article does not verify. [32]

Iran International's headline list says two political prisoners whose murder death sentences were overturned were moved to solitary confinement on 22 November, raising fears of execution on another charge. [18]

Iran International reports a dispute over who will lead state TV, one sign of unresolved institutional control. [41]

IranWire's April account describes residents paying heavily for internet, rising prices and anxiety about income. [32]

Iran International's headline list reports Tehran's warning over the Armenian corridor and renewed threats against European bases, with a claimed missile range of 4,500 km that the outlet questions. [18]
international_md:
Reuters reports talks that ended without a breakthrough, and Al Jazeera reports continued US and Iranian strikes around Qeshm Island and the Gulf. [3][16][4]

Bloomberg reports the IAEA's inability to account for the stockpile, and Al Jazeera reports the referral vote. [7][21]

Lloyd's List Intelligence and Al Jazeera report the redirected ships, mine strikes and reduced transits. [23][4]

AFP, Reuters and Al Jazeera report inflation above 80 percent, record currency lows and winter gas shortages. [27][29][9]

AFP and Al Jazeera carry the competing protest death counts, and Euronews carries the Boroumand Center's execution count. [33][8][36]

Reuters reports a quiet street and officials who fear unrest driven by gas shortages and prices. [9]

VOA and The National report the Afghan deportations and the minority crackdown using UN figures. [44][43]

Reuters and Al Jazeera report Gulf attacks, Chinese and Russian opposition to new strikes and the mediation channels. [3][4]
scholar_md:
Critical Threats (AEI and ISW) assesses that securing recognition of Iranian control over Hormuz is an Iranian war aim and found nothing significant to report on US and Iran talks on 17 November. [5]

The Arms Control Association records the NPT withdrawal bill, the lack of excavation at bombed sites and no sign of weaponization. [6]

Andreas Krieg of King's College London called the task force a desperate attempt to extend the naval blockade by land, and Matthew Savill of RUSI expects reliance on satellite imagery, drones and financial intelligence. [24]

The IMF's April forecast, as reported by Amwal Al Ghad, sees a 6.1 percent contraction in 2026. [31]

The UN fact-finding mission, as reported by the International Business Times, found crimes against humanity against protesters and perceived dissenters. [34]

Critical Threats documents preemptive deployments and the Abdanan rally, and Al Jazeera quotes analyst Negar Mortazavi saying the leader's absence is unusual but imposed by circumstance. [5][10]

The WHO situation report is the main technical source on attacks on health care and medicine shortages. [42]

Al Jazeera's analysts say the task force cannot seal Iran's land borders without Caspian access or troops on the ground. [24]
